lesson.title: Running Off the Chart: Infinite Discontinuity
lesson.summary: An infinite discontinuity occurs when a function's values grow without bound as x approaches a point from one or both sides, producing a vertical asymptote rather than a finite jump or a simple hole.
lesson.body:
A discontinuity at c is called an infinite discontinuity when at least one of the one-sided limits, lim(x to c-) f(x) or lim(x to c+) f(x), is infinite, meaning the function increases without bound toward positive infinity or decreases without bound toward negative infinity as x approaches c from that side. Because an infinite limit is not a real number, it does not satisfy the ordinary definition of a limit existing, so the two-sided limit at c fails to exist and c is a genuine discontinuity, even in cases where the function heads to the same infinite value from both sides.

This is the same behavior already introduced as an infinite limit, now viewed through the lens of continuity: wherever a function has an infinite limit at some point c, that point is automatically a discontinuity of f, since f(c) is typically undefined there and no finite limit exists to match it anyway. Graphically, an infinite discontinuity almost always corresponds to a vertical asymptote, a vertical line x = c that the graph hugs more and more tightly without ever touching, since the function's values are shooting off toward infinity rather than approaching any fixed height.

Worked example: let f(x) = 1/x and examine x = 0. Approaching from the right, x is a small positive number, so 1/x is a large positive number, and lim(x to 0+) 1/x = positive infinity. Approaching from the left, x is a small negative number, so 1/x is a large negative number, and lim(x to 0-) 1/x = negative infinity. Both one-sided limits are infinite, and they even head in opposite directions, so f has an infinite discontinuity at x = 0, with a vertical asymptote along the line x = 0.

A second example shows that both sides can also agree on the same infinite direction and still count as an infinite discontinuity. Let g(x) = 1/(x - 2)^2. Near x = 2, the denominator (x - 2)^2 is always positive and shrinking toward zero, whether x approaches from the left or the right, so g(x) grows arbitrarily large and positive from both directions: lim(x to 2-) g(x) = positive infinity and lim(x to 2+) g(x) = positive infinity as well. Even though both one-sided limits agree on heading to positive infinity, positive infinity is still not a real number, so the limit still fails to exist in the required sense, and x = 2 is still an infinite discontinuity, with a vertical asymptote there too.

Infinite discontinuities are easy to distinguish from jump discontinuities by checking whether the one-sided limits are finite numbers or not. If both one-sided limits exist as ordinary, finite numbers that merely disagree, the discontinuity is a jump. If at least one side is unbounded, growing or shrinking without any ceiling or floor, the discontinuity is infinite instead. Rational functions are the most common source of infinite discontinuities, and they occur exactly at the real zeros of the denominator that are not also zeros of the numerator, which is why examining where a denominator vanishes is usually the fastest way to locate one.
